failures.title: BMW B47TU2 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: EGR Cooler and Exhaust System Faults - 2019-Present
items.whatHappens: While significantly refined over the earlier B47D20A, the B47TU2 still carries an EGR cooler that can develop internal micro-fractures under sustained high-load use. Symptoms include unexplained coolant loss, occasional white exhaust smoke, and EGR-related fault codes on the dashboard. The risk is lower than on pre-2019 B47 units, but remains the most documented issue on this revision.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, an EGR cooler replacement or system blanking (where legally compliant) is a manageable repair. If severe coolant ingress has caused hydrolock, a full B47TU2 engine replacement becomes necessary.

items.title: 48V Mild-Hybrid System Faults - 2019-Present
items.whatHappens: Most B47TU2 applications are paired with a 48V belt-driven starter-generator (BSG) and a small lithium-ion battery. Early reports from high-mileage units point to BSG failures and 48V battery degradation, presenting as intermittent stop-start faults, "drivetrain fault" warnings, or the engine refusing to restart after auto-stop. These are electrical/hybrid-system issues rather than core engine failures, but they require BMW-specific diagnostic equipment to resolve.
items.repairVsReplace: The 48V system components are typically serviced separately from the engine itself. A full B47TU2 engine replacement is rarely required for mild-hybrid faults alone, but any replacement engine must be confirmed compatible with the host vehicle's 48V architecture.

failures.goodYearsLine: The B47TU2 is widely regarded as the most reliable iteration of BMW's 2.0-litre diesel to date. The rear-mounted timing chain vulnerability that plagued the N47 family was resolved when the B47 moved the chain to the front in 2014, and the TU2 revision further strengthens this arrangement. Catastrophic engine failure is rare on this code when serviced to BMW's Longlife-04 oil specification .

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the B47TU2
variants.intro: The B47TU2 engine code is stamped directly onto the engine block, typically on a machined pad adjacent to the oil filter housing or on the front timing cover. It is also explicitly listed on your vehicle's V5C registration document under the engine details section, or it can be definitively verified via a VIN decode through a BMW specialist or the vehicle's iDrive service menu. The B47TU2 is most commonly confused with the earlier B47D20A, the higher-output B47D20B, the detuned B47D20D, and the transverse-platform variants B47C20U0 and B47C20U1. While these share the same 2.0-litre diesel architecture, fitting the wrong revision to a B47TU2 host will almost always cause issues: the B47TU2 is uniquely calibrated for 48V mild-hybrid integration, and its ECU mapping, BSG loom, and mounting orientation differ from earlier B47 variants. A non-TU2 unit dropped into a G-series mild-hybrid host will throw persistent drivetrain faults and will not integrate with the 48V system.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement B47TU2 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used B47TU2 is a challenging purchase due to the engine's current-production status - supply is scarce and most salvage units come from write-offs with unknown 48V system history. Only consider a used B47TU2 if it carries a full BMW service history, the 48V BSG has been tested, and the EGR cooler shows no signs of weeping.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned B47TU2 is the most balanced choice for most owners. A reputable rebuild will address the EGR cooler with an updated unit, verify the 48V BSG integration points, and replace all critical seals and gaskets, directly resolving the engine's most documented issues while restoring factory compression.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for high-value G-series hosts such as the G20 3 Series or G30 5 Series, where long-term ownership is planned. An upgraded rebuild should include a revised EGR setup, verified 48V system compatibility, and potentially a remapped ECU to maximise longevity and efficiency.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting your B47TU2 through our vetted network ensures the work is completed by BMW specialists familiar with the mild-hybrid integration, backed by a minimum 12-month warranty and nationwide delivery options.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: For typical host vehicles like the G20 3 Series, G30 5 Series, and G01 X3, current market values range from £18,000 to £45,000. A reconditioned B47TU2 replacement sits comfortably within this value band, making it a financially sound investment. Even for earlier G-series hosts valued around £14,000, the combination of strong retained values and the B47TU2's inherent reliability keeps the replacement cost well within the viable threshold.

items.question: What is the most common problem with the B47TU2 engine?
items.answer: The most documented issues are EGR cooler micro-fractures causing coolant leaks, and 48V mild-hybrid system faults such as belt-driven starter-generator failures. Typical onset for EGR issues is between 60,000 and 120,000 miles. Symptoms include unexplained coolant loss, white exhaust smoke, or intermittent stop-start and drivetrain fault warnings. Unlike the older N47, the front-mounted timing chain is highly reliable and rarely causes catastrophic failure.

items.question: Which BMW models use the B47TU2 engine?
items.answer: The B47TU2 is fitted across BMW's latest G-series and newer F-series LCI models from 2019 onwards, primarily powering 18d and 20d badges with 48V mild-hybrid systems. Common hosts include the 3 Series (G20), 5 Series (G30 LCI/G60), X1 (U11), and X3 (G01 LCI). Always verify your specific chassis code and engine stamping before ordering a replacement unit.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned B47TU2 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned B47TU2 is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the known EGR cooler vulnerabilities and the complexity of the 48V mild-hybrid system. A proper rebuild will address the EGR cooler with an updated unit, verify the 48V BSG integration points, and replace all critical seals. A used engine inherits the exact same EGR and hybrid system risks, and sourcing a low-mileage used TU2 is difficult given its current-production status.
